title: 4.3 · Secret messages (Spotting tricks, ciphers)
name: Secret messages (Spotting tricks, ciphers)
summary: Students learn the signs of a trick message: hurry, a prize, a request for private information, a sender they do not know. In Packet Post's Spot the Trick they tap the cues on each card and choose safe, trick or ask for help; then, for fun, they make and read a secret message on a cipher wheel. Pairs share one device.
iCan: spot the signs of a trick message
say what to do: do not reply, and tell a trusted adult
make and read a secret message with a cipher wheel (for fun)
materials: Cipher Wheels printable (one per pair, with a paper fastener)
Trick or Treat cards and a printed cue checklist
doNow: A message says: You won a free tablet! Reply with your mailbox key to claim it. What do you do?
plan: Explore: vote safe or trick on three cards, then the cipher wheel

warmup.why: two retrieval items from 4.2, one vocabulary item, one preview of today, one more from 4.2

do: Open Packet Post at Spot the Trick on the projector (Open game at this chapter). Show card 1. The class votes with thumbs: up for safe, down for trick. Tap the cues the class finds, then choose. Do cards 2 and 3 the same way.
Hold up a paper cipher wheel. Turn it 3 and decode a short word with the class.
say: Real companies never ask for your passphrase. A message that says hurry, you won, or reply with your key is a trick.
When in doubt, do not reply and do not tap. Tell a trusted adult.
ask: What gave card 1 away? Which word or button made you suspicious?
explore.afterAsk: List the cues on the board as they come: hurry, a prize, asks for private information, a sender you do not know. Leave the list up during Play.
explore.bigIdea: Real companies never ask for your passphrase; when in doubt, ask a trusted adult.

play.stretch: all 6 cards, then Secret Messages levels 1-3 for fun
play.pairs: driver and navigator on one device; swap at the chime every 2 cards; the navigator reads the card out loud and names a cue before the driver chooses
lookFors: calling a message safe because it has a friendly picture or a name they know
choosing safe for a message that only asks you to tap a button
never choosing the ask-for-help answer, even when unsure
play.misconception: A trick message does not look scary: it looks friendly and exciting, and the sign is what it asks for, like hurrying or private information.
earlyFinishers: help a neighbor without touching their screen

discuss: Which cue gave the trick away most often?
What do you do when you are not sure a message is safe?
showMe: One pair shows a card they got wrong on the projector; the class finds the cue they missed.

exit.sentencePrompt: What does a trick message often do, and what should you do when you get one?
exit.frame: A trick message often ___, so I ___.

rubric.line: Spotting trick messages and what to do
levels: Names one sign of a trick message
Names a sign and says what to do: do not reply, tell a trusted adult
Names two or more signs and explains why a real company would not ask

exit.paper: exit half-sheet (two per page) with the three items and the sentence frame

support: a printed cue checklist on the desk: hurry, prize, private information, unknown sender
hint 1 circles the part of the card to read again
stretch: write a secret message on the cipher wheel for a neighbor pair to decode

unpluggedTwin.title: Cipher Wheels and Trick or Treat
materials: Cipher Wheels printable and a paper fastener per pair
steps: Pairs sort the Trick or Treat cards into safe and trick, and circle the cue on each trick card.
Check together with the cue checklist; for every trick card, say what to do.
Build the cipher wheel. One partner turns it to a key and writes a short word in code; the other decodes it with the same key.
Share: why can only the person with the key read the message?

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: a message says you won a free tablet and asks you to reply with your mailbox key to claim it. What do you do?

Play Packet Post, chapter Spot the Trick, in pairs for 20 minutes. Classes, then the lesson, then Play. If the game asks, the quest code is 5 1 0 0. Goal: 4 cards. No warm-up and no projector needed; playing signed out is fine.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it.

shortPeriod40.discuss: Which cue gave the trick away most often?
shortPeriod40.keep: the exit ticket is never cut

add: the Cipher Wheels and Trick or Treat twin (15 minutes) before Play
the secret message swap after Play
10 minutes of the Unit 4 review on Brain Board

notes: Senders on the cards are roles (Prize Team, Your bank) and buttons are verbs (Claim now); no real names appear.
The cipher wheel is for fun: it is not part of the exit evidence for this band, though one exit item asks why the key keeps a message private.
Never use the words a trick message uses to ask for a passphrase; the Do Now says mailbox key on purpose.
Shared devices: this is an odd lesson in the unit, so partner A signs in; the gradebook and the Standards tab count the signed-in student.

steps.title: Today
steps.body:
Do Now: A message says: You won a free tablet! Reply with your mailbox key to claim it. What do you do?

Big idea: Real companies never ask for your passphrase; when in doubt, ask a trusted adult.

We will talk about:
- Which cue gave the trick away most often?
- What do you do when you are not sure a message is safe?

steps.title: Warm-up (live)
steps.body: Five quick questions. Your teacher shows them on the projector or starts them live.

steps.title: Play: Spot the Trick
steps.body:
Goal: 4 cards. Stretch: all 6 cards. Then the game takes you to secret messages, just for fun.
If the game asks for a quest code, it is 5 1 0 0.
Pairs: driver and navigator. Swap when you hear the chime. The navigator reads the card out loud and names a clue.

steps.title: Exit ticket
steps.body: Three quick questions about trick messages.
